name: Rudder Pyre
geological_features: A network of lava rivers following ancient tectonic grooves across the surface
Vast ash plains interspersed with hardened lava domes
Fumarole fields releasing jets of superheated steam and toxic gas
specific_features: Extremophilic microbial mats that burn with a visible blue flame when exposed to the atmosphere
description: Rudder Pyre is a medium volcanic world whose surface is etched with a network of lava rivers that follow ancient tectonic grooves like channels carved by a deliberate hand. The rivers flow from highland volcanic sources to lowland lava seas, their courses so regular and parallel that early observers mistook them for artificial canals. Ash plains stretch between the lava channels, their grey surfaces broken by hardened lava domes that rise like blisters from the tortured landscape.

The toxic atmosphere is thick with volcanic gases and heated by the radiant energy of the surface below, creating a permanent greenhouse effect that keeps temperatures lethally high even in the cooler highland regions. Fumarole fields hiss and rumble across the ash plains, their steam plumes adding moisture to the otherwise dry atmosphere and creating localized fog banks that glow orange from the reflected light of nearby lava. The planet smells of sulfur and hot metal, a combination that corrodes equipment and spirits in equal measure.

The microbial life on Rudder Pyre is remarkable for its metabolism — the organisms oxidize atmospheric sulfur compounds so aggressively that their biofilms ignite with a pale blue flame when exposed to oxygen-rich gas mixtures. This pyrophilic biology has fascinated xenobiologists, but the organisms are increasingly rare, their habitat shrinking as volcanic activity shifts and the chemical balance of their environment changes. They may represent a form of life adapted to conditions that are themselves temporary.

Rudder Pyre's geological activity is driven by tidal interactions with a binary companion that has been slowly spiraling away over geological time, reducing the tidal heating that powers the volcanism. Models predict that the planet will cool significantly over the next few hundred million years, potentially becoming habitable by current definitions. For the microbial life that depends on the current volcanic chemistry, however, the cooling trend is an extinction event in slow motion — their world is dying even as it becomes more welcoming to others.
